messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: partial eval gradients for normal_log
parts:
The new normal_log is in place. This speeds up normal_log
itself by a factor of nearly 4 when all arguments are var.
Matt tested something similar in the context of the Rats
model and found it was a little more than twice as fast
with partially evaluated normal gradients.

This is a fair bit of rewriting per distribution, but
it only requires a single function for all 2**K ways
a function with K scalars can be instantiated.

The rest of this message is just a walkthrough of the code
for normal_log.

The main thing to look at is the top-level implementation
of normal_log in:

prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal.hpp

Here's the critical definition, which I documented in the
code as an example of how to do the other probability functions.
I'll insert some more comments here. The declaration hasn't
changed from before (though it was already more than a mouthful):

template <bool Prop,
typename T_y, typename T_loc, typename T_scale,
class Policy>
typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T_y,T_loc,T_scale>::type
normal_log(const T_y& y, const T_loc& mu, const T_scale& sigma,
const Policy& /*policy*/) {
static const char* function = "stan::prob::normal_log<%1%>(%1%)";

There are some more using statements:

using std::log;
using stan::is_constant;
using stan::math::check_positive;
using stan::math::check_finite;
using stan::math::check_not_nan;
using stan::math::value_of;
using stan::math::simple_var;
using stan::prob::include_summand;

The next block returns if there's nothing to calc.

// check if no variables are involved and prop-to
if (!include_summand<Prop,T_y,T_loc,T_scale>::value)
return 0.0;

Recall that include_summand is a metaprogram evaluating to true
if either !Prop or one of the other types is a var.

Next, set all the arguments to double values using the overloaded
function value_of (defined in math/special_functions for doubles
and agrad/special_functions for var):

// pull out values of arguments
const double y_dbl = value_of(y);
const double mu_dbl = value_of(mu);
const double sigma_dbl = value_of(sigma);

Note that the log prob accumulator is now a double rather than a var:

// set up return value accumulator
double logp(0.0);

So that tests are all on doubles now:

// validate args
if (!check_not_nan(function, y_dbl, "Random variate y", &logp,
Policy()))
return logp;
if (!check_finite(function, mu_dbl, "Location parameter, mu,",
&logp, Policy()))
return logp;
if (!check_positive(function, sigma_dbl, "Scale parameter, sigma,",
&logp, Policy()))
return logp;

Next, I declared wide-scoped variables to hold derivatives, initialized
with dummy values to stop the compiler from griping.

// declare derivatives -- don't need values
double d_y(0.0);
double d_mu(0.0);
double d_sigma(0.0);

Next are terms that appear in multiple log prob and gradient
calcs. Compute them once and store.

// reusable subexpression values
const double inv_sigma = 1.0 / sigma_dbl;
const double y_minus_mu_over_sigma
= (y_dbl - mu_dbl) * inv_sigma;
const double y_minus_mu_over_sigma_squared
= y_minus_mu_over_sigma * y_minus_mu_over_sigma;

static double NEGATIVE_HALF = - 0.5;

Log probability is just as before, with metaprogram include_summand
instantiating value to true if the term should be included

// log probability
if (include_summand<Prop>::value)
logp += NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI;
if (include_summand<Prop,T_scale>::value)
logp -= log(sigma_dbl);
if (include_summand<Prop,T_y,T_loc,T_scale>::value)
logp += NEGATIVE_HALF * y_minus_mu_over_sigma_squared;

Now we do the same thing for the gradients, calculating them only
if the relevant term is a stan::agrad::var (i.e., not is_constant).
Keep in mind that all calcs and returns are on double values:

// gradients
if (!is_constant<T_scale>::value)
d_sigma = -inv_sigma + inv_sigma * y_minus_mu_over_sigma_squared;
if (!is_constant<T_loc>::value)
d_mu = inv_sigma * y_minus_mu_over_sigma;
if (!is_constant<T_y>::value) {
if (!is_constant<T_loc>::value)
d_y = - d_mu;
else
d_y = - inv_sigma * y_minus_mu_over_sigma;
}

Finally, return a new var with appropriate precomputed
partial derivatives. See below for details on the simple_var
function.

return simple_var(logp,y,d_y,mu,d_mu,sigma,d_sigma);
}


The value_of() function has an implementation and template
specialization for double values in stan/math/special_functions:

namespace stan { namespace math {

template <typename T>
inline double value_of(T x) {
return static_cast<double>(x);
}

template <>
inline double value_of<double>(double x) {
return x;
}

Then there's an overload (NOT a template specialization)
in stan/agrad/special_functions:

namespace stan { namespace agrad {

inline double value_of(const agrad::var& v) {
return v.vi_->val_;
}

As with the other functions, we rely on argument-dependent
lookup to find this overload and use it for var arguments.
So you need to be careful to include agrad/special_functions
as there is no stan/agrad/prob/distributions/...

The implementation of simple_var() for doubles is in
stan/math/special_functions:

namespace stan { namespace math {

inline double simple_var(double v,
double /*y1*/, double /*dy1*/,
double /*y2*/, double /*dy2*/,
double /*y3*/, double /*dy3*/) {
return v;
}

This just returns v, so the other arguments aren't needed (but the
skeleton needs to be there to make the function match). This and
the double-based value_of() function were critical for not having
a dependency from stan::prob to stan::agrad.

The function simple_var is overloaded for all 7 possible var
instantiations in stan/agrad/partials_vari.hpp.
Here are the first two cases; others are similar:

namespace stan { namespace agrad {

inline agrad::var simple_var(double v,
const agrad::var& y1, double dy1,
const agrad::var& y2, double dy2,
const agrad::var& y3, double dy3) {
return agrad::var(new agrad::partials3_vari(v,
y1.vi_, dy1,
y2.vi_, dy2,
y3.vi_, dy3));
}

inline agrad::var simple_var(double v,
const agrad::var& y1, double dy1,
const agrad::var& y2, double dy2,
double /*y3*/, double /*dy3*/) {
return agrad::var(new agrad::partials2_vari(v,
y1.vi_, dy1,
y2.vi_, dy2));
}

Finally, there's the partialsN_vari classes. Here's the
partials3_vari case:

class partials3_vari : public vari {
private:
vari* operand1_; const double partial1_;
vari* operand2_; const double partial2_;
vari* operand3_; const double partial3_;
public:
partials3_vari(double value,
vari* operand1, double partial1,
vari* operand2, double partial2,
vari* operand3, double partial3)
: vari(value),
operand1_(operand1), partial1_(partial1),
operand2_(operand2), partial2_(partial2),
operand3_(operand3), partial3_(partial3)
{ }
void chain() {
operand1_->adj_ += adj_ * partial1_;
operand2_->adj_ += adj_ * partial2_;
operand3_->adj_ += adj_ * partial3_;
}
};

All it does is store the partials and operand and then
apply the chain rule directly in its chain() method.

You might also want to look at normal_test.cpp in the tests.
It evaluates all possible combinations using a templated test
function and a simple implementation of normal_log I stripped
out of our previous implementation for testing. The tests
use a bit more overload and template specialization trickery,
but I hope it's (relatively) clear after the above.

- Bob
